objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain the instruments, their errors and the cross-check used in a constant airspeed descent, fly the entry, the straight and turning descent and the level-off solely by instruments while talking a learner through them, and spot and fix the errors learners make under a view-limiting device.
why: In a descent the airspeed, the vertical speed and the altitude are all changing at once, and during the change the attitude indicator is the only flight instrument that gives a positive attitude reference [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]. Pilots without instrument training, or whose skills have eroded, lose control in about 10 minutes once they must rely on instruments alone [[24:366|AFH 18-17]], so the descent habits you build under the hood may one day keep a learner alive. The CFI standard for this Task is also tighter than the one your private learners fly to.

prereading.what: Straight climbs and descents: the descent entry, constant airspeed versus constant rate, both level-off techniques and the 11 common errors. The core of this lesson.
prereading.label: IFH 7-14 to 7-19

prereading.what: Standard rate turns, bank rule of thumb, rollout lead, climbing and descending turns, and the pitch and bank errors in turns.
prereading.label: IFH 7-19 to 7-25

prereading.what: The same descent on a glass panel: entry, the 10 percent lead, power before pitch at level-off, and the glass error list.
prereading.label: IFH 7-49 to 7-51

prereading.what: Control and performance, primary and supporting, pitch, bank, power and trim instruments, cross-check methods and errors, and instrument interpretation.
prereading.label: IFH 6-2 to 6-14

prereading.what: How the pitot-static and gyro instruments work and the errors each one has.
prereading.label: IFH 5-3 to 5-22

prereading.what: VSI trend, rate and lag, and what blocked pitot and static systems do to the instruments in a descent.
prereading.label: PHAK 8-7 to 8-12

prereading.what: Vestibular illusions: the graveyard spiral, Coriolis and the somatogravic illusion from a quick throttle reduction.
prereading.label: IFH 3-5 to 3-6

warmup: Think first: your learner is under the hood at 4,500 feet. She pulls the throttle back and pushes the nose down in one quick motion. The airspeed jumps 12 knots, the VSI swings past 1,200 fpm down and then settles near 700, and the heading has drifted 15° left. At 3,600 feet she adds cruise power for a 3,500 foot level-off, the nose comes up, and she stops at 3,560. What went wrong at the entry, why did the heading move, what really caused the high finish, and which of these would you fix first?

key_terms.def: Controlling the aircraft's position in space by instruments instead of outside visual references [[23:134|IFH 6-1]].
Control instruments (attitude and power indicators) show attitude and power directly; performance instruments (altimeter, airspeed, VSI) show what the airplane is actually doing [[23:135|IFH 6-2]].

In the primary and supporting method, the instrument with the most pertinent information for pitch, bank or power at that moment; the airspeed tape is primary for pitch in a constant airspeed descent [[23:143|IFH 6-10]] [[23:211|IFH 7-50]].
The other instruments, which help keep the important ones at their desired indications [[23:143|IFH 6-10]].
Power reduced to a predetermined setting with pitch adjusted to hold the airspeed; any airspeed deviation calls for a pitch change [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].
Same entry, but once the VSI stabilizes near the desired rate it is primary for pitch and the airspeed indicator is primary for power [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].
The continuous and logical observation of instruments for attitude and performance information, also called scanning [[23:143|IFH 6-10]].
Understanding how each instrument is built and works, then applying that to the airplane, the maneuver and the conditions [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].

The time for the VSI to reach its full deflection after a change; it grows with the speed and size of the pitch change [[23:139|IFH 6-6]]. The needle usually settles in 6 to 9 seconds [[1:210|PHAK 8-8]].
The miniature aircraft's wings and center dot on the attitude indicator, about 2° of pitch [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].
Starting the level-off before the altitude; the amount depends on descent rate and technique, for example 100 to 150 feet at 500 fpm for a level-off at cruise speed [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].
Letting the nose pitch up at the level-off because forward pressure is not held as power is added [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

chunks.title: What each instrument tells you in a descent

body.p: Function and operation. Interpretation starts with knowing how each instrument is built and how it works [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. Your learner met these instruments in level flight; in a descent each one does a specific job.

head: Instrument
How it works
Its job in this descent
rows: Attitude indicator
A gyro with a vertical spin axis in a double gimbal; the airplane pitches and rolls around it [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]
The only instrument that shows the actual attitude directly and instantly [[23:140|IFH 6-7]]; every pitch change is made on it [[23:140|IFH 6-7]]
Airspeed indicator
Measures dynamic pressure: pitot (ram) pressure compared with static pressure [[23:103|IFH 5-8]]
Primary for pitch in a constant airspeed descent [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]; very little lag [[23:139|IFH 6-6]]
Vertical speed indicator
Aneroid and case both vented to static, the case through a calibrated orifice, so case pressure changes more slowly [[23:103|IFH 5-8]]
Trend first (needle direction), then the stabilized rate [[1:210|PHAK 8-8]]
Altimeter
A stack of aneroid capsules that change thickness as pressure changes [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]
The only exact altitude information [[23:140|IFH 6-7]]; tells you when the lead point arrives
Heading indicator
A gyro with a horizontal spin axis; not north-seeking, so it is set to the compass [[23:114|IFH 5-19]] [[23:115|IFH 5-20]]
Primary for bank in straight flight [[23:143|IFH 6-10]]
Turn coordinator
Senses rotation about both the roll and yaw axes; no pitch information [[23:117|IFH 5-22]]
Primary for bank once a standard rate turn is set [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]
Tachometer or manifold pressure
Engine instruments that show the power set [[23:141|IFH 6-8]]
Set the predetermined descent power; not affected by turbulence, trim or control pressure [[23:137|IFH 6-4]]

body.p: Indication of the aircraft attitude. The attitude indicator shows pitch directly; the altimeter, VSI and airspeed indicator show it indirectly [[23:137|IFH 6-4]]. To judge bank, interpret the heading indicator, turn coordinator and attitude indicator together [[23:147|IFH 6-14]]. A rapid change in airspeed means a large pitch change and a slow change means a small one [[23:139|IFH 6-6]].

The descent twist. Until the airplane settles at a constant airspeed and attitude, the airspeed indicator, altimeter and VSI all show changing values, and during that transition the attitude indicator is the only flight instrument giving a positive attitude reference [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]. In the matching climb text the airspeed becomes primary for pitch once the airplane is stabilized [[23:175|IFH 7-14]], and the glass section names the airspeed tape primary for pitch in this descent [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]. So: fly the entry on the attitude indicator, then let the airspeed tell you whether the attitude is right.

callout.text: Set attitude and power on the control instruments, trim, then read the result on the performance instruments and adjust [[23:135|IFH 6-2]] [[23:136|IFH 6-3]].

check.q: Ten seconds into the entry your learner corrects pitch every time the VSI needle moves. Why is the VSI a poor pitch reference right then?
check.a: During the transition the airspeed, altimeter and VSI are all still changing, and only the attitude indicator gives a positive attitude reference; the VSI also lags behind the real change [[23:177|IFH 7-16]] [[23:139|IFH 6-6]].

chunks.title: Instrument limitations and errors on the way down

body.p: Instrument limitations and potential errors. A descent exposes several of them at once, because pressure, speed and attitude are all changing. Teach each one with what it means for this maneuver.

head: Instrument
Limitation or error
What it means in a descent
rows: VSI
Lags behind the real change; lag grows with the speed and size of the pitch change [[23:139|IFH 6-6]]. Rough control and turbulence lengthen the lag and make the needle erratic [[1:210|PHAK 8-8]]
Do not chase it during the entry. In turbulence take the average of the swings as the reading [[23:138|IFH 6-5]] [[23:139|IFH 6-6]]
VSI out of calibration
May show a small climb or descent in level flight; treat that reading as its zero [[23:139|IFH 6-6]] [[1:210|PHAK 8-8]]
Judge the descent rate from the displaced zero, not the painted one
Attitude indicator
Slight nose-up indication in rapid acceleration and nose-down in rapid deceleration; small pitch and bank error after a 180° turn, gone within about a minute [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]
Confirm the picture with the other pitch instruments after slowing to descent speed and after long turns
Miniature aircraft setting
Set at cruise speed in level flight and not moved for other speeds, so the instrument shows a true pitch picture [[23:138|IFH 6-5]]
A learner who re-centers it in the descent hides the real attitude
Heading indicator
Drifts about 15° per hour; compare with the compass at least every 15 minutes [[23:115|IFH 5-20]]
Reset it in steady straight flight before the descent
Magnetic compass
Errors in climbs, descents, power changes, airspeed changes and turbulence [[23:140|IFH 6-7]]
Not a reference to set anything by during the descent itself
Altimeter
Colder than standard air: true altitude is lower than indicated [[23:100|IFH 5-5]]
Less terrain clearance at the bottom of the descent than the dial suggests

body.p: Blocked pitot tube. If the ram opening and drain hole are both blocked, the airspeed indicator works like an altimeter [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]. In a descent the rising static pressure makes it show a decrease in airspeed even though the real speed has not changed [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]. Application: a learner flying the airspeed as primary pitch would lower the nose to 'fix' it and the real speed would build.

Blocked static system. The altimeter freezes at the altitude where it blocked, the VSI reads zero, and below that altitude the airspeed reads faster than actual [[23:98|IFH 5-3]] [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]. Application: in a descent that false high airspeed invites the learner to raise the nose and slow down. With the alternate static source open, the altimeter reads slightly high, the airspeed reads high and the VSI shows a momentary climb [[23:98|IFH 5-3]].

callout.text: When one instrument disagrees with the rest, cross-check before you move the controls: several instruments that agree are worth more than one alone [[23:221|IFH 7-60]].

check.q: In a stabilized 90 knot descent the airspeed starts to fall while the attitude indicator, the VSI and the rate of altimeter unwinding all stay the same. What should the learner suspect before touching the pitch?
check.a: An airspeed system fault such as a blocked pitot tube, which shows a falling airspeed in a descent. The other pitch instruments do not agree, so do not lower the nose to chase it [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]] [[23:221|IFH 7-60]].

chunks.title: Cross-check in the descent: fixation and omission

body.p: Proper instrument cross-check techniques. Cross-check and interpretation are the two fundamental skills of attitude instrument flying [[23:143|IFH 6-10]]. No single method is required: look at the instruments that give the best information for that phase, usually the ones being held constant, and use the rest to keep them there [[23:143|IFH 6-10]].

bullets: Selected radial: 80 to 90 percent of the time on the attitude indicator, quick glances out to the others, always returning through the attitude indicator [[23:144|IFH 6-11]].
Inverted-V: attitude indicator to turn coordinator, back up, down to the VSI, back up [[23:144|IFH 6-11]].
Rectangular: across the top row and back along the bottom; it gives every instrument equal weight and so takes longer to return to the one that matters most [[23:144|IFH 6-11]].

head: Phase
Where the eyes should be
rows: Entry

Attitude indicator for the pitch change; the power instrument only long enough to set the predetermined power [[23:177|IFH 7-16]] [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]; heading, since power and pitch changes are when heading errors start [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Stabilized straight descent
Airspeed for pitch, heading indicator for bank, tachometer or manifold pressure for power, as in the matching climb [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]
Descending turn
Faster cross-check for bank as well as pitch [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]; turn coordinator once the bank is set [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]
Level-off
Altimeter and VSI for the lead, then an accelerated cross-check until established in straight-and-level flight [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]

body.p: Fixation and omission. Fixation is staring at one instrument; the IFH example is a pilot staring at an altimeter 200 feet low while tension on the controls lets the heading wander [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. Omission is leaving an instrument out, such as not checking the heading indicator after a rollout [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. A third fault, emphasis, is relying on the one instrument the pilot understands best [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. Application in this Task: fixation on the airspeed during the entry while the heading drifts, and omission of the altimeter until the lead point is gone.

callout.text: Failing to vary the rate of cross-check during power or attitude changes and descent entries is a listed error [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. In a standard rate turn of 90°, the heading indicator can be left out for about 20 seconds after the turn is set, since the lead point is not near yet [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

check.q: Your learner sets descent power, then watches the tachometer until it reads exactly the target while the nose drifts low. What is the error and what does the IFH say about it?
check.a: Fixation on the power instrument. A small power error matters less than large altitude and heading errors, and staring at the gauge does not make the airplane slow down faster [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].

chunks.title: Entering the descent: power, pitch and trim

body.p: The IFH entry works with or without an attitude indicator. First slow to the chosen descent airspeed in straight-and-level flight. Then reduce power further to a predetermined setting, and as the power comes back lower the nose to keep the airspeed constant. Trim off the control pressures [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. The glass section says the same: if the power is reduced and pitch is not lowered at the same time, the airspeed keeps decaying below the target [[23:211|IFH 7-50]].
Control application solely by reference to instruments:

bullets: Make every pitch change on the attitude indicator, whichever instrument showed the need [[23:140|IFH 6-7]].
Use very light pressure; the horizon bar should move no more than half a bar width at a time [[23:138|IFH 6-5]].
Apply small pressures smoothly, cross-check quickly for the result, and continue only as the instruments confirm it; small changes are easy to stop and correct [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].
Move the throttle by the amount experience says is needed, then cross-check the power indicator to refine it, without fixating on it [[23:137|IFH 6-4]].
A power change can move the airplane about all of its axes [[23:141|IFH 6-8]], so check heading during the power reduction; failing to is a listed heading error [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].

body.p: Trimming the aircraft. The airplane is trimmed when it holds the desired attitude with all control pressures neutralized [[23:141|IFH 6-8]]. Set the attitude with control pressure first, then trim; using trim alone to change attitude gives erratic control [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]. Trim often and in small amounts, and center the ball with rudder trim if the airplane has it [[23:174|IFH 7-13]] [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]. Unless the airplane is trimmed, the pilot cannot tell whether a pressure change comes from the airplane or from his or her own hands [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

Why trim makes this maneuver easy: in a trimmed airplane, even a small power reduction lets the nose drop just enough to hold the trimmed airspeed, and the airplane descends at a rate in proportion to the thrust removed [[24:369|AFH 18-20]]. Pitch is holding the airspeed and power is setting the descent.

callout.text: Failure to learn and use proper power settings is a listed error [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. Know your trainer's descent power for each airspeed you teach before the first hood lesson; the POH or your own test flights supply it.

check.q: Your learner reduces power and pushes the nose down at the same moment, straight from cruise speed. What does the IFH entry do differently?
check.a: It first slows to the descent airspeed in straight-and-level flight, then reduces to a predetermined power while lowering the nose just enough to keep that airspeed, then trims [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

chunks.title: Holding the descent: interpretation and corrections

body.p: Instrument Interpretation. The same attitude gives very different performance in different airplanes: the IFH example shows a trainer and a jet with an identical picture on the attitude indicator, the trainer climbing at 500 fpm and 90 knots and the jet at 2,000 fpm and 250 knots [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. For each maneuver, learn what performance to expect and which instruments to read for it [[23:147|IFH 6-14]].

head: You see
It means
Correction
rows: Airspeed above target
The pitch attitude is too low [[23:139|IFH 6-6]]
Raise the miniature aircraft slightly on the attitude indicator and recheck the airspeed [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]
Airspeed below target
The pitch attitude is too high [[23:139|IFH 6-6]]
Lower the miniature aircraft slightly and recheck
Airspeed changing fast
A large pitch change has happened [[23:139|IFH 6-6]]
Look for the cause: a bump, a held pressure, a trim change
Airspeed right, descent rate not what was planned
Power is not giving the planned rate; the rate follows the thrust removed [[24:369|AFH 18-20]]
Adjust power and keep holding the airspeed with pitch; check both before moving anything [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]
Repeated small turns the same way
Out of trim with a wing-low tendency [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Trim the cause out instead of correcting heading again and again

body.p: Constant airspeed versus constant rate. In this Task the airspeed is the target, so any airspeed deviation calls for a pitch change. In a constant rate descent the entry is the same, but the VSI becomes primary for pitch once it settles near the rate and the airspeed indicator becomes primary for power [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]. Keep them apart in the learner's mind; mixing them is how a learner ends up raising the nose to 'fix' a descent rate and losing the airspeed.

callout.text: Before every entry, have the learner say the numbers she expects: airspeed, power and roughly what rate. Interpretation is comparing what you see with what you expected for that maneuver [[23:147|IFH 6-14]].

check.q: Holding 90 knots at the briefed descent power, the learner gets 700 fpm when she wanted 500. Should she raise the nose?
check.a: No. In a constant airspeed descent pitch holds the airspeed, so raising the nose would cost airspeed. The rate follows the thrust removed, so add a little power and keep 90 knots with pitch [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[24:369|AFH 18-20]].

body.p: The ACS asks for the descent in straight flight and in turns. The IFH method is to combine the straight descent technique with turn technique, allow for the effect of the turn on lift and power, and speed up the cross-check because both bank and pitch are now changing [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

bullets: Standard rate is 3° per second, a full circle in 2 minutes [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. Approximate bank: divide the true airspeed by 10 and add half the result; at 100 knots about 15°, at 120 knots about 18° [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

Roll in with coordinated aileron and rudder; set the approximate bank on the attitude indicator, then keep it with the turn coordinator as primary for bank and the attitude indicator as supporting [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Learners commonly roll in much too fast [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

Bank reduces the vertical lift component [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Application: with the airspeed held by pitch, expect the descent rate to increase a little in the turn rather than chasing it with the nose.
Roll out at the same rate you rolled in and lead the heading by half the bank angle [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. For small heading changes, use no more bank than the degrees to be turned [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].
During the rollout the attitude indicator is primary for bank; once the wings are about level, the heading indicator takes over [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

After the rollout, if the heading keeps changing while the attitude indicator shows wings level: with the ball centered the gyro has precessed; with the ball off center the airplane is slipping or skidding. Center the ball, stop the heading change and retrim [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

body.p: Pitch errors the IFH lists for turns all show up here: preoccupation with bank during entry and recovery, not adjusting pitch as the vertical lift component changes, changing pitch before it is needed, not trimming in a prolonged turn, and dropping the straight-and-level cross-check after a perfect rollout [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

callout.text: A prolonged, coordinated descending turn is the graveyard spiral set-up: the pilot loses the sensation of turning, feels a level descent, and pulls back, which tightens the spiral [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. Keep practice turns to modest heading changes until the learner's cross-check is quick.

check.q: At 100 knots true airspeed the learner starts a standard rate descending turn from 270° to 180°. About what bank, and at about what heading does the rollout start?
check.a: About 15° (100 / 10 = 10, plus half, 5). Lead by half the bank, about 7 or 8°, so start the rollout passing about 187° [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

chunks.title: Leveling off at the assigned altitude

body.p: The level-off must start before the altitude. The lead depends on the descent rate and the control technique, and with too little lead the airplane overshoots unless the technique is rapid [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

head: Level-off
Lead
Technique
rows: At a cruise speed higher than descent speed (analog section)

Add cruise power at the lead point. The nose tends to rise as speed builds, so hold forward pressure to keep the descent rate until about 50 feet above, then smoothly set the level attitude [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]
At the descent airspeed (analog section)
About 50 feet [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]
Raise the nose to the level attitude and add power to hold the airspeed at the same time; trim and return to the straight-and-level cross-check [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]
Back to cruise (glass section)
10 percent of the descent rate: 100 feet at 1,000 fpm [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]

Increase power to cruise first, then raise the pitch toward level; avoid rapid changes that could cause control problems or spatial disorientation; let the airplane accelerate and adjust power [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]
At constant airspeed (glass section)
Not given as a number [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]
Raise pitch with a smooth, coordinated power increase to a predetermined value, since pitch alone adds drag and loses speed; trim [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]

body.p: Two errors live here. Ballooning is letting the nose pitch up as power goes in, because forward pressure was not held [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. The other is not recognizing the approaching straight-and-level indications; keep an accelerated cross-check until positively established in straight-and-level flight [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

callout.text: CFI ACS AI.XI.C.S3: "Level off at the assigned altitude and maintain altitude ±100 feet, heading ±10°, and airspeed ±10 knots." The Private ACS (PA.VIII.C.S3) allows ±200 feet and ±20° for the same Task, with the same ±10 knots. Your learners train to the Private numbers; you are held to the tighter ones while you teach.

check.q: Descending at 500 fpm and 90 knots, the learner must level at 3,000 feet and stay at 90 knots. Where does she start and what moves together?
check.a: About 50 feet above, near 3,050: raise the nose to the level attitude and add power to the setting that holds 90 knots at the same time, then trim [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

chunks.title: Risk: the hazards of flying on instruments

head: Hazard
What the sources say
What it means for this Task
rows: Failure to maintain VFR

A VFR pilot who cannot keep attitude by the natural horizon is in IMC, whatever the weather, and should treat it as an emergency [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]. Attempting VFR into IMC is one of the most common causes of fatalities [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]
Tell every learner that this hood training does not prepare them for marginal weather or IMC [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]
Spatial disorientation

The inner ear cannot sense slight or steady attitude changes and creates false sensations [[24:367|AFH 18-18]]. A quick throttle reduction can create the somatogravic illusion, and the pilot may pull into a nose-up or stall attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]
The descent entry is a power reduction: teach it smooth, and teach the learner to believe the instruments
Loss of control

Untrained or rusty pilots lose control in about 10 minutes on instruments alone [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]. Combined maneuvers such as descending turns compound the problem for an untrained pilot [[24:370|AFH 18-21]]
Descending turns are the hardest part of this Task; build up to them
Fatigue
Degrades attention and concentration, impairs coordination and the ability to communicate; with acute fatigue, stay on the ground [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]
Hood work is mentally tiring; keep sessions short and watch for skill fatigue
Stress
When stress exceeds a person's ability to cope, performance falls off rapidly; such a pilot should not fly [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]
A tense learner grips the yoke; a person cannot feel control pressures with a tight grip [[24:367|AFH 18-18]]
Emergency off airport landings

A precautionary landing, with power and time to choose a site, is less hazardous than a forced landing; the non-instrument-rated pilot trapped by weather who never considers one accepts an extremely hazardous alternative [[24:350|AFH 18-1]]
Teach the descent to a safe altitude as part of a plan that may end in a precautionary landing below the weather

callout.text: The IFH warns against rapid changes at the level-off because they can lead to control problems or spatial disorientation [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]. Smooth power changes at both ends of the descent protect the learner's inner ear as well as the altitude.

check.q: Why does the IFH single out a quick throttle reduction as a hazard for a pilot without outside references?
check.a: The rapid deceleration can create the somatogravic illusion, and the disoriented pilot may pull the aircraft into a nose-up or stall attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

chunks.title: Risk: asking for help and avoiding traffic

body.p: When to seek assistance or declare an emergency. An aircraft is in at least an urgency condition the moment the pilot is doubtful about position, fuel, weather or anything else that could affect safety, and that is the time to ask for help [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. A non-instrument-rated pilot who cannot continue in VFR conditions should tell the controller, say there is no instrument rating, and declare a distress condition [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]]. Squawk 7700 and then establish communications [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2]]; MAYDAY begins a distress call and PAN-PAN an urgency call [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]]. If a controller's urgency starts to rush a descent or turn, it is reasonable to ask the controller to slow down [[24:370|AFH 18-21]].

Collision hazards. Simulated instrument flight requires a safety pilot in the other control seat holding at least a private pilot certificate with the category and class ratings for the aircraft [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109]], with adequate vision forward and to each side, or a competent observer to supplement it [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109]]. AC 90-48E warns instructors and safety pilots against preoccupation with instruction and against the tendency to look inside excessively during simulated instrument flight [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]].

bullets: In the midair study the AIH cites, a flight instructor was aboard in 37 percent of the accidents, and most happened at or near nontowered airports below 1,000 feet [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].
Practice see and avoid at all times, under VFR or IFR [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].
A descent points the airplane toward traffic at lower altitudes; application: brief the practice area away from arrival paths and clear below before every entry.

callout.text: While the learner is under the hood, you are the only eyes outside. Talk the learner through the descent from what you see outside, and glance at the panel only as often as the teaching needs.

check.q: Under the hood, your learner's descending turn goes well and you spend a whole minute watching her scan. Which two habits does AC 90-48E warn about?
check.a: Preoccupation with instruction at the expense of constant vigilance for traffic, and looking inside excessively during simulated instrument flight [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]].

body.p: Distractions. The AIH's list of distractions for training includes having the learner climb 200 feet and hold it, then descend 200 feet and hold it [[25:180|AIH 9-10]], which is this Task in miniature. Interruptions are a significant source of errors: a learner may return to the wrong step [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

Task prioritization. Attend to the most important tasks first [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. Before a learner combines tasks, each one should be practiced until it can be done reasonably well in isolation [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. For this Task: straight descents before descending turns, and level-offs at descent speed before level-offs to cruise.

Loss of situational awareness. Forgetting the heading being turned to is likely when the maneuver is rushed [[23:186|IFH 7-25]], and failing to note the descent rate for the lead gives overshoots or undershoots [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. Have the learner say the assigned altitude, heading and lead point out loud.

Disorientation. In a turn, a head movement in a different plane can trigger the Coriolis illusion, so build a cross-check with little head movement and pick up dropped items with minimal head motion [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

Fixation and omission, from the instructor's seat. Beginning instrument pilots characteristically fixate on particular instruments, and fixation often means the task has not had enough practice in isolation [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. Follow the learner's eyes: a long look at one instrument suggests fixation, and eyes that never reach the engine instruments suggest inattention, but looking is not the same as seeing [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].

callout.text: Add distractions only once the straight descent is solid, and keep head-down ones out of the descending turns because of the Coriolis risk [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

check.q: Your learner's eyes stay locked on the airspeed indicator for long stretches of the descent. What does that suggest, and what is a likely root cause?
check.a: Possible fixation, which is often a sign that the task has not been practiced enough in isolation [[25:82|AIH 3-31]] [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

head: Stage
What happens in this Task
rows: Ground brief

The instruments and their errors, primary and supporting for entry, descent and level-off, the trainer's descent power, the level-off lead, and the point that hood work does not prepare the learner for IMC [[25:181|AIH 9-11]] [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]
Build on what is known

Straight-and-level and climbs on instruments come first (AI.XI.A, AI.XI.B); a learner who has flown visual descents (AI.VIII.D) already knows the control inputs. Known to unknown, simple to complex [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]; new learning rests on a solid base [[25:91|AIH 3-40]]
Demonstrate
Fly it on instruments while explaining the power settings and attitudes, in the same order as your explanation [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]
Learner tells, you fly
Hear the learner call the entry sequence, the expected numbers and the lead before she is busy flying [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
Learner flies under the view-limiting device
A hood or other view-limiting device [[23:11|IFH viii]]; straight descents, then turns, then level-offs at both speeds; be ready to take control on first attempts [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
Debrief
Learner self-assessment, then your assessment and comparison [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]

bullets: Integrated instruction: instrument references from the first time a maneuver is introduced, with identical control inputs either way [[25:180|AIH 9-10]] [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].
Let the learner go part way into an error when it is safe, such as a mild balloon at a high practice altitude, so she finds the way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].
If the descent looks good but you doubt the understanding, vary it: a different airspeed, the other turn direction, a level-off at descent speed instead of cruise [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

For private learners, also teach the AFH emergency version: power in 100 RPM or 1 inch steps, no more than 500 fpm, nose no more than one bar width below level, and avoid descending turns [[24:369|AFH 18-20]] [[24:370|AFH 18-21]]. The Private lesson (PA.VIII.C) covers it.

callout.text: Before every entry, have the learner brief four items: target airspeed, descent power, heading, and the level-off altitude with its lead point. It turns the AIH's 'learner tells' step into a habit.

check.q: Why make the learner master straight constant airspeed descents before adding turns?
check.a: Tasks should be done reasonably well in isolation before they are combined, or fixation follows; and the turn adds bank control, which needs a faster cross-check [[25:81|AIH 3-30]] [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

body.p: The IFH lists 11 common errors in straight climbs and descents [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[23:180|IFH 7-19]], a glass-panel version [[23:211|IFH 7-50]] [[23:212|IFH 7-51]] and pitch errors in turns [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. For S4 the examiner may fly some of them: name the error, its cause and its fix.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Overcontrolling pitch on entry
Large pitch changes, VSI swinging past the target
Small, smooth pressures; cross-check for the result before adding more [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]
Not varying the cross-check rate
Errors build during power and attitude changes
Speed up the scan during every change and entry [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]
Not holding the new pitch attitude
Nose wanders after each correction
Hold it and trim, so the correction can be judged [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]
Not trimming off pressures
Pressure held, erratic pitch
Trim; otherwise pilot and airplane inputs cannot be told apart [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]
Not knowing power settings
Repeated power hunting
Learn and use the descent power settings [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]
Not cross-checking both airspeed and VSI before adjusting
The wrong control used for the deviation
Check both; a change in one may correct the other [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]
Chasing the VSI
Pitch following the needle
Change pitch on the attitude indicator; the VSI confirms [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]
No lead from the descent rate
Overshoot or undershoot of the altitude
Note the rate and start the level-off at the lead [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]
Ballooning
Nose rises as cruise power goes in
Hold forward pressure as power is added [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]
Poor pitch and power coordination on a slow-speed level-off
Airspeed sags at the level-off
Pitch and power together; pitch before power adds drag [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]
Not recognizing the approaching level indications
Drift after an otherwise good level-off
Accelerated cross-check until established [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]
Pitch not adjusted as the vertical lift component changes in turns
Rate changes at roll-in, altitude gained or lost at rollout
Anticipate the pitch change with bank [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Preoccupation with bank during turn entry and recovery
Pitch drifts while rolling
Check pitch, power and trim as bank pressures start [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]

body.p: Analyze before you correct. When the learner thinks aloud you can tell whether the error comes from a misconception or from motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. In this Task the classic misconception is mixing the constant rate and constant airspeed methods; the classic motor-skill problem is overcontrolling pitch.

callout.text: Rehearse each S4 answer in three parts: 'I see..., because..., so we...'.

check.q: Each time the VSI passes 500 fpm the learner raises the nose, and the airspeed keeps sagging below target. What is the error and the fix?
check.a: Chasing the VSI, from not cross-checking it against the other pitch instruments. In a constant airspeed descent the airspeed decides pitch, and pitch is changed on the attitude indicator [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:212|IFH 7-51]] [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

Tags mark the attitude indicator as supporting pitch and bank, the VSI as primary pitch, the heading indicator as primary bank and the turn coordinator as supporting bank.

Other tags mark the airspeed indicator as primary power, the attitude indicator as supporting pitch and bank, the heading indicator as primary bank, the turn coordinator as supporting bank and the VSI as supporting pitch.

f3.alt: Side view of two climb paths from the same point over the ground. A small airplane climbs gently to the left, with its airspeed indicator and VSI drawn at the left edge; a jet climbs steeply to the right toward 10,000 feet, with its airspeed indicator and VSI at the right edge. One attitude indicator at the bottom shows the same nose-up picture for both. Labels read 7 1/2 miles, 25 miles and 5-minute climb.

scenario.title: Hood descents on a hazy afternoon
scenario.setup: You are a CFI with a private pilot learner on her second hood lesson in a fixed-pitch trainer with a six-pack panel. The plan: constant airspeed descents at 90 knots from 5,500 to 2,500 feet, with standard rate descending turns, leveling off at cruise speed. There is light turbulence and haze, and the practice area sits under a route used by traffic arriving at a nontowered airport. At the ramp she mentions she worked a double shift and slept four hours.

questions.q: What do you do about her double shift and short night?
questions.a: Acute fatigue degrades attention, coordination and communication, and the PHAK says to stay on the ground with it; hood work is mentally demanding, so reschedule [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]].

questions.q: On the rescheduled flight the VSI swings between 300 and 900 fpm down in the bumps. How should she read it?
questions.a: Take the average of the fluctuations as the correct reading [[23:138|IFH 6-5]] [[23:139|IFH 6-6]], and lean on the altimeter, which is less sensitive than the VSI [[23:139|IFH 6-6]].

questions.q: Every descent she finishes 10 to 15° left of heading, and she keeps correcting right. What do you look for?
questions.a: Heading errors start during power and pitch changes, and repeated corrections for the same drift point to an untrimmed wing-low tendency; teach her to check heading through the power reduction and trim out the cause [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].

questions.q: After rolling out of a descending left turn, the attitude indicator shows wings level but the heading keeps moving left with the ball centered. What is happening?
questions.a: The attitude gyro has precessed. Stop the heading change with the heading indicator, check the attitude indicator, and retrim [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]; such errors correct themselves within about a minute [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].

questions.q: Halfway down you realize you have watched her scan for over a minute. Why is that a problem here?
questions.a: Instructors and safety pilots tend to look inside excessively during simulated instrument flight [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]], and midairs cluster near nontowered airports below 1,000 feet with an instructor often aboard [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. Under an arrival route, your eyes belong outside.

questions.q: She levels off for 2,500 feet, heading 090°, and ends at 2,630 feet on 105° at 92 knots. How do you grade it against her standard and yours, and what likely caused the altitude miss?
questions.a: Within the Private ACS (±200 feet, ±20°, ±10 knots) but outside the CFI ACS limits of ±100 feet and ±10°. Ending high after adding cruise power points to ballooning, not holding forward pressure as power went in [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

skills.do: Transition to the descent pitch attitude and power setting on an assigned heading using proper instrument cross-check and interpretation, and coordinated flight control application, while explaining it: slow to descent speed in level flight, reduce to the predetermined power, lower the nose on the attitude indicator to hold the airspeed, check heading through the power change, and trim.
skills.practice: Fly the entry with a safety pilot while talking through each step, and note your trainer's power and attitude for each descent speed [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

skills.do: Descend at a constant airspeed to specific altitudes in straight flight and turns: hold the airspeed with small pitch changes on the attitude indicator, use standard rate turns with the turn coordinator as primary bank, and explain why the cross-check speeds up in the turn.
skills.practice: Practice straight descents first, then standard rate descending turns both ways, rolling out on headings with a half-bank lead [[23:185|IFH 7-24]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

skills.do: Level off at the assigned altitude and maintain altitude ±100 feet, heading ±10°, and airspeed ±10 knots, explaining the lead you chose and why the nose wants to rise as power comes in.
skills.practice: Level off both at descent airspeed (about 50 foot lead) and at cruise (100 to 150 feet at 500 fpm) until both finish inside the CFI tolerances [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

skills.do: Analyze and correct common errors related to this Task: when the examiner, playing a learner, overcontrols the entry, chases the VSI, forgets the lead or balloons at the level-off, name the error, its cause and the fix.
skills.practice: Learn the IFH error lists with a 'what you see' and a fix for each, and have another CFI applicant fly them for you under the hood [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

quiz.q: What is the first step of the IFH method for entering a constant airspeed descent?
options: Slow to the descent airspeed while holding straight-and-level flight
Lower the nose one bar width and let the airspeed settle
Reduce power to idle and pitch for the 500 fpm target rate
Retrim nose down so the airplane starts the descent by itself
quiz.why: First reduce airspeed to the descent airspeed in straight-and-level flight, then reduce power further and lower the nose to hold that speed [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

quiz.q: The pitot tube and its drain hole both ice over. As the airplane descends, the airspeed indicator shows:
options: No change, because the trapped pitot pressure stays constant
A higher airspeed than the airplane is really flying
A lower airspeed even though the real speed has not changed
Zero, because the pitot and static pressures equalize
quiz.why: With the pitot system sealed, rising static pressure in a descent compresses the diaphragm and the indicator shows a decrease [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]].

quiz.q: After a steady pitch change, about how long does a standard VSI take to settle on the new rate?
options: Under 1 second
About 2 to 3 seconds
15 to 20 seconds
About 6 to 9 seconds
quiz.why: The needle stabilizes after a short period, 6 to 9 seconds; that delay is the lag [[1:210|PHAK 8-8]].

quiz.q: During a rapid deceleration, what error can a gyro attitude indicator show?
options: A slight nose-up indication
A slight nose-down indication
A false bank toward the left wing
A tumble once pitch passes about 60°
quiz.why: There may be a slight nose-up indication in rapid acceleration and a nose-down indication in rapid deceleration [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].

quiz.q: What does the IFH name as the weakness of the rectangular cross-check?
options: It never includes the turn coordinator or the VSI
It is only usable with a glass primary flight display
It takes longer to return to the instrument that matters most
It keeps the eyes on the attitude indicator 80 to 90 percent of the time
quiz.why: By giving every instrument equal weight, the rectangular scan lengthens the time to get back to the critical instrument [[23:144|IFH 6-11]].

quiz.q: Why does the IFH say a pilot needs to give the power indicators little attention once descent power is set?
options: Turbulence, trim and control pressure do not change their readings
They lag several seconds behind any throttle movement
They read high whenever the alternate static source is open
They are backed up by the airspeed indicator in every phase
quiz.why: Power indicators are not affected by turbulence, improper trim or inadvertent control pressures, so in most aircraft little attention keeps the setting constant [[23:137|IFH 6-4]].

quiz.q: Rolling out of a descending turn in a 16° bank, how far before the heading should the rollout start?
options: 16°, the full bank
4°, a quarter of it
12°, three quarters
8°, half the bank angle
quiz.why: Lead the desired heading by about half the bank angle used [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

quiz.q: A quick throttle reduction without outside references may cause which illusion and reaction?
options: Inversion illusion; pushing abruptly into a nose-low attitude
Somatogravic illusion; pulling up toward a stall
Coriolis illusion; rolling into a bank opposite the real one
The leans; leaning toward the bank that was entered slowly
quiz.why: Rapid deceleration from a quick throttle reduction can make the disoriented pilot pull into a nose-up or stall attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

quiz.q: AC 90-48E says simulated instrument flight brings what tendency for instructors and safety pilots?
options: Talking too much, so the learner misses the ATC calls on frequency
Letting the learner fly too long without breaks
Looking inside too much and forgetting to see and avoid
Leaving the hood on below 1,000 feet AGL
quiz.why: During simulated instrument flight there is a tendency to look inside excessively and forget see-and-avoid duties [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]].

quiz.q: After squawking 7700 in a distress or urgency condition, what does the AIM say to do next?
options: Switch to 121.5 MHz and wait for ATC to call you
Establish communications with the ATC facility right away
Set the transponder to standby to cut frequency noise
Keep silent and follow whatever vectors appear on the moving map
quiz.why: Squawk 7700 with Mode C and then immediately establish communications with the ATC facility [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2]].

final_quiz.q: On your CFI checkride you level off for an assigned 3,000 feet, heading 090° and 90 knots, and hold 3,110 feet, 095° and 82 knots. Which value is outside the AI.XI.C.S3 tolerance?
options: The heading, which is 5° off
The airspeed, which is 8 knots slow
Nothing; all three are within limits
The altitude, 110 feet high
final_quiz.why: The CFI ACS allows ±100 feet, ±10° and ±10 knots, so only the 110 foot altitude error is out. The lead technique that prevents it is on [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

final_quiz.q: A learner's descents keep drifting left, and she corrects right again and again without the drift stopping. What fault does the IFH describe?
options: Not finding the cause of the earlier error, such as a wing-low trim condition
Rolling into the corrections with too steep a bank for the size of the heading change
Reading the heading indicator backwards, so each correction goes the wrong way
Setting the heading indicator from the compass while in the descent
final_quiz.why: Failure to note the cause of a previous heading error, for example an out-of-trim left wing low tendency, leads to repeated corrections while trim is ignored [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].

final_quiz.q: After a descending left turn, the attitude indicator shows wings level, the heading indicator keeps moving left, and the ball is centered. What is the best interpretation?
options: The airplane is skidding, so more right rudder is needed
The heading indicator has drifted and needs resetting to the magnetic compass now
The attitude gyro has precessed; stop the heading change and retrim
The turn coordinator has failed, since it shows no turn
final_quiz.why: If heading changes with the attitude indicator level and the ball centered, the gyro has precessed; stop the heading change and retrim [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

final_quiz.q: Descending from 6,000 feet, the static port ices over at 5,000. Continuing down to 4,000, what does the learner see?
options: Altimeter stuck near 4,000, VSI normal, airspeed reading low
Altimeter stuck near 5,000, VSI at zero, airspeed reading high
Altimeter and VSI normal, airspeed reading zero
Altimeter high, VSI a brief climb, airspeed normal
final_quiz.why: Trapped static pressure freezes the altimeter at the blockage altitude, the VSI reads zero, and below that altitude the airspeed reads faster than actual [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]] [[23:98|IFH 5-3]].

final_quiz.q: Returning to a 500 fpm descent after a drift, the learner's correction shows 750 fpm on the VSI. What does this indicate?
options: A normal correction while the VSI catches up with its lag
An out-of-calibration VSI that should be read from its offset zero
Turbulence, so the average of the swings should be used
Overcontrolling: over 200 fpm beyond the desired rate
final_quiz.why: When the VSI shows more than 200 fpm beyond the rate desired, overcontrolling is indicated [[23:139|IFH 6-6]].

final_quiz.q: On a PFD, the learner descends at 600 fpm toward 5,000 feet and wants cruise speed after leveling. Which plan matches the glass section of the IFH?
options: At about 5,060, add cruise power first, then raise the pitch
At about 5,060, raise the pitch to level first, then add the cruise power
At 5,000 exactly, raise the pitch quickly to stop the descent
At about 5,300, reduce the descent rate to 200 fpm, then level
final_quiz.why: Lead by 10 percent of the rate (600 x 0.10 = 60 feet) and increase power to cruise before increasing pitch toward level [[23:211|IFH 7-50]].

final_quiz.q: In haze, your learner (hood off) has been in a long, gentle descending turn. She says she feels level but sinking and starts to pull back. What should you teach?
options: Pull harder, since the descent is the only real problem
Add power first and keep the turn going until the sinking stops
Level the wings on the attitude indicator before raising the nose
Look outside for the horizon and fly by feel until the haze clears up
final_quiz.why: This is the graveyard spiral: pulling back in the turn tightens the spiral and increases the altitude loss [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. Believe the instruments and level the wings first [[24:367|AFH 18-18]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner trims well in level flight but holds forward pressure through the whole descent. What problem does the IFH say this creates?
options: The VSI lag becomes longer and less predictable
She cannot tell her own inputs from the airplane's
The attitude indicator precesses whenever pressure is held on the yoke
The airspeed indicator over-reads when the elevator is deflected
final_quiz.why: Unless the airplane is trimmed, it is difficult to tell whether control pressure changes come from aerodynamic changes or from the pilot [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

final_quiz.q: You glance at your learner and see her eyes fixed on the airspeed indicator, never moving to the engine gauges in a 3 minute descent. What does the AIH say this suggests?
options: Fixation on one instrument and possible inattention to the engine
Good selected-radial technique for this maneuver
Emphasis, since the airspeed is the primary pitch instrument in this descent
Nothing; eye direction tells an instructor nothing
final_quiz.why: A long look at one instrument suggests fixation, and eyes that never go to the engine instruments suggest inattention, though looking is not the same as seeing [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].

final_quiz.q: You plan hood work in a low-wing trainer, and the learner's hood blocks your view to the left. Under 14 CFR 91.109, what makes the flight legal?
options: A hood with a side window cut out for the instructor's use
A transponder and ADS-B Out, so ATC can watch for traffic
Flying only in Class B or C airspace with radar service
A competent observer aboard to supplement your vision from the right seat
final_quiz.why: The safety pilot needs adequate vision forward and to each side, or a competent observer who adequately supplements it [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109]].

final_quiz.q: In a constant airspeed descent at 90 knots, the learner sees 85 knots and 650 fpm with the planned power set. What is the right correction?
options: Add power to bring the airspeed back up to 90 knots right away
Lower the nose slightly on the attitude indicator and recheck
Raise the nose to cut the descent rate back toward the planned 500 fpm
Add nose-up trim to slow the descent
final_quiz.why: In a constant airspeed descent any airspeed deviation calls for a pitch adjustment; low airspeed means the pitch is too high, so lower it slightly [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[23:139|IFH 6-6]].

final_quiz.q: Heading 305° in a descent, the learner is told to turn to 110°. Using the IFH reciprocal shortcut, which way is shorter?
options: Left, because 110 is smaller than 305
Either way, since the change is exactly 180°
Right, because the reciprocal of 305 is 125 degrees
Left, because the reciprocal of 305 is 105
final_quiz.why: 305 - 200 + 20 = 125, the reciprocal; 110 lies before 125 going right, so turn right [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

final_quiz.q: Ending her descent, the learner adds cruise power at the lead point and the nose rises, and she stops 50 feet above the altitude. What was missing?
options: Forward pressure to hold the descending attitude
A larger lead of at least 300 feet at that descent rate
Nose-up trim before the power was added
A check of the magnetic compass during the level-off
final_quiz.why: Ballooning comes from failing to keep the descending attitude with forward-elevator pressure as power is increased to cruise [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

takeaways: During the entry only the attitude indicator gives a positive attitude reference; once stable, airspeed is primary for pitch.
Entry: slow to descent speed in level flight, reduce to a known power, lower the nose to hold the speed, trim.
In a constant airspeed descent, airspeed errors are fixed with pitch; the descent rate comes from the power.
Descending turns: standard rate, bank about 15 percent of true airspeed, faster cross-check, rollout lead of half the bank.
Lead the level-off: about 50 feet at descent speed, 100 to 150 feet at 500 fpm to cruise, or 10 percent of the rate on glass; hold forward pressure as power comes in.
Know what a blocked pitot or static system does in a descent before you trust a single instrument.
Under the hood you are the only eyes outside; the CFI standard is ±100 feet, ±10° and ±10 knots.
cfi_notes: The IFH gives three level-off leads: 100 to 150 feet at 500 fpm when leveling to cruise and about 50 feet at descent speed in the analog section [[23:178|IFH 7-17]], and 10 percent of the rate in the glass section [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]. At 500 fpm the 10 percent rule gives only 50 feet for the cruise level-off. Teach one method consistently and tell the learner the other exists.

The two sections also differ in sequence for the cruise level-off: the analog text adds power at the lead and holds forward pressure until about 50 feet above [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]; the glass text says increase power before increasing pitch [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]. They agree on the idea; the analog one is more specific about ballooning.

IFH Figure 7-30 is captioned 'Constant airspeed descent, airspeed high, reduce power', but its tags mark the VSI as primary pitch and the airspeed indicator as primary power, which is the constant rate method described in the text above it [[23:179|IFH 7-18]] [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. Do not use it to teach the constant airspeed descent.

The analog descent text never names the airspeed indicator as primary for pitch in so many words; it says any airspeed deviation calls for a pitch adjustment [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. The climb text [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] and the glass descent text [[23:211|IFH 7-50]] do name it. Teaching it as primary is consistent with all three.

The AFH emergency descent for untrained pilots in IMC (cruise airspeed, power in 100 RPM steps, no more than 500 fpm, one bar width) is a different procedure from this Task's constant airspeed descent [[24:369|AFH 18-20]]. Teach both and always say which one you are teaching.

The IFH says the heading indicator can be left out of the scan for about 20 seconds in a 90° standard rate turn [[23:186|IFH 7-25]] and about 25 seconds in its chapter 6 example [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. Both make the same point; do not let a learner memorize either as a fixed number.
The somatogravic illusion is tied to a quick throttle reduction [[23:73|IFH 3-6]], which is exactly how learners tend to start a descent. Teach a smooth power reduction from the first lesson.
The AIH asks you to make sure learners understand that instrument introduction does not prepare them for IMC [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. Say it at every hood lesson, not only the first.

You are usually the safety pilot as well as the instructor. AC 90-48E names looking inside during simulated instrument flight as a specific instructor weakness [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]]; plan the lesson so your teaching does not need your eyes on the panel.
gaps: Descent power settings and pitch attitudes for a specific trainer come from the POH/AFM or your own flight tests; the IFH gives none for a light single in a descent.
The CFI ACS gives tolerances only after the level-off (S3); no source gives a tolerance for the airspeed or heading during the descent itself.
The IFH does not describe a constant airspeed descending turn step by step; it says only to combine the straight descent and turn techniques.
No source gives a limit on how long or how far to practice descending turns under the hood, or a minimum practice altitude for this Task.
The sources do not describe how to demonstrate an instrument descent from the right seat, where the instruments are seen at an angle; that is CFI technique.

activities.title: Instrument and its job
activities.intro: Tap an instrument, then tap how it works or what it does in this descent.

pairs.r: Vertical-axis gyro; the only direct, instant attitude picture
Pitot pressure against static; primary pitch once stable
Case vented through a calibrated leak; trend, then rate
Aneroid capsules; the only exact altitude
Senses roll and yaw; no pitch information
Horizontal-axis gyro; drifts about 15° per hour

activities.title: True or false: errors on the way down
activities.intro: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

cards.s: With the static port blocked, the airspeed indicator reads lower than actual as the airplane descends below the blockage altitude.
cards.why: False. Below the blockage altitude it reads faster than actual [[23:98|IFH 5-3]] [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]].

cards.s: With the alternate static source open, the altimeter reads slightly higher than the actual altitude.
cards.why: True. Cabin pressure is lower, so the altimeter reads slightly high and the airspeed reads high [[23:98|IFH 5-3]].

cards.s: Attitude indicator errors after a 180° turn stay until the gyro is caged and reset.
cards.why: False. They are small and correct themselves within a minute or so of straight-and-level flight [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].

cards.s: A VSI that shows 100 fpm down in level flight can still be used if that reading is treated as zero.
cards.why: True. Consider the error when using it; any change from that reading shows a pitch change [[23:139|IFH 6-6]].

cards.s: The magnetic compass is a good reference for setting the heading indicator during a descent.
cards.why: False. The compass has errors in climbs, descents, power and airspeed changes [[23:140|IFH 6-7]].

activities.intro: Drag each label to its numbered pin on the IFH example of one attitude in two airplanes.

activities.title: Descent and turn numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: On a PFD you descend at 1,200 fpm toward 6,000 feet and will return to cruise. Using the IFH 10 percent rule, at what altitude do you start the level-off?
About what bank angle gives a standard rate turn at 90 knots true airspeed?
Your learner levels off 150 feet below the assigned altitude. What VSI rate should her climb back show?
items.why: The correction rate should be about twice the altitude error: 150 x 2 = 300 fpm [[23:139|IFH 6-6]].

items.q: She is regaining altitude at a planned 400 fpm. Above what VSI reading is she overcontrolling?
items.why: More than 200 fpm beyond the desired rate shows overcontrolling: 400 + 200 = 600 fpm [[23:139|IFH 6-6]].

items.q: How many seconds does a standard rate descending turn take to change heading by 90°?
items.why: Standard rate is 3° per second: 90 / 3 = 30 seconds [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

activities.title: From cruise, down, and level at cruise
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order (IFH 7-17), then tap Check.
steps: Slow to the descent airspeed in straight-and-level flight
Reduce to the predetermined descent power and lower the nose to hold the airspeed
Hold the airspeed with small pitch changes on the attitude indicator
Note the descent rate to choose the lead
At the lead point, add cruise power and hold forward pressure
About 50 feet above, ease to the level attitude and keep a fast cross-check

activities.title: Constant airspeed or constant rate?
activities.intro: Tap each statement, then tap the descent it belongs to (IFH 7-17, 7-50).

items.t: The airspeed indicator is primary for pitch
Any airspeed deviation calls for a pitch change
The VSI becomes primary for pitch once it settles near the rate
The airspeed indicator is primary for power
Entry: reduce to a predetermined power while lowering the nose
During the transition, only the attitude indicator gives a positive attitude reference

activities.title: Under the hood from 5,500 feet
activities.intro: You are the CFI and safety pilot. Your learner is under the hood at 5,500 feet and 110 knots, heading 090°, to descend at 90 knots, turn to 180° on the way, and level at 3,500 feet at cruise speed.

steps.s: The learner reaches for the throttle and starts pushing the nose over.
options: Push over to the descent picture now and fix the speed later
Stop and slow to 90 knots in level flight first
Pull the throttle to idle for a faster descent
Retrim nose down and let the airplane find a speed
steps.why: The IFH entry first slows to the descent airspeed in straight-and-level flight, then reduces power while lowering the nose [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

steps.s: Ten seconds into the entry the VSI reads 300 fpm and is still moving. The learner pushes for more.
options: Good; 500 fpm is the target, so keep pushing
Add power so the needle settles faster
Hold the attitude; the VSI lags and is still settling
Switch the scan to the compass for heading
steps.why: The VSI lags behind the real change, and during the transition only the attitude indicator gives a positive reference [[23:139|IFH 6-6]] [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

steps.s: Stabilized: 96 knots and 600 fpm down at the briefed power.
options: Reduce power until the airspeed reads 90
Raise the nose about half a bar width and recheck
Ignore it; the ACS gives no tolerance in the descent
Lower the nose to drive the rate to 700
steps.why: High airspeed means the pitch is too low; correct on the attitude indicator by no more than half a bar width [[23:139|IFH 6-6]] [[23:138|IFH 6-5]].

steps.s: Rolling into the turn to 180° at about 90 knots true airspeed, the learner sets 25° of bank.
options: Shallow to about 13 or 14° and confirm standard rate on the turn coordinator
Keep 25° to finish the turn sooner
Roll out and do the turn after the level-off
Steepen to 30° and reduce power
steps.why: Standard rate bank is about 15 percent of true airspeed, 90 / 10 + 4.5 = 13.5°, held with the turn coordinator [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

steps.s: Wings level at 180°, passing 3,620 feet at 500 fpm, she plans the level-off to cruise.
options: Wait until 3,500 and pull firmly to level
Add power at 3,520 and raise the nose together
Lower the nose to keep 90 knots until 3,550
Add cruise power now and hold forward pressure until about 3,550
steps.why: At 500 fpm, add cruise power 100 to 150 feet above, hold forward pressure to keep the rate, and level smoothly at about 50 feet above [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].
